title: Women of the McLoughlin House (Self-Guided Outside Tour)
topics: Burial, Cemetery and Gravesite;Colonization and Settlement;Commerce;Trade;Forts;Women's History
accessibility: Three of the four stops on this tour can be accessed via paved sidewalks. The tour route includes some stairs between Stops 1 and 2, which can be bypassed via a detour described in the directions provided. Visitors will experience slight changes in elevation when visiting Stop 2 - the McLoughlin gravesite. To access Stop 3 - The Fountain, visitors must cross a grassy park. For visitors who are unable to cross this uneven surface, the fountain is visible from Stop 2 - the McLoughlin gravesite. Visitors can return to the sidewalk along Center Street and proceed to Stop 4 from there.
short_description: This short, self-guided walking tour of the McLoughlin House Unit of Fort Vancouver National Historic Site, located in Oregon City, Oregon, takes you to four different landmarks and offers an overview of the women who lived in these homes and worked to preserve them.

title: Hike the Buffalo Point Campground Trails
accessibility: These trails are narrow in places and traverses steep, uneven, and rocky terrain.
short_description: The Buffalo Point Campground Trails give campers, day hikers, and leashed dogs a chance to stretch their legs between the campground and the historic cabin area at Buffalo Point. Hike through a mix of a pine and oak trees, a cedar glade, and past a sinkhole as you explore. Wildflowers dot the trail system throughout the spring and summer. Finally, the view from the Overlook Trail is one that you do not want to miss!

title: Hike the Rush Mine Level Trail and Morning Star Interpretive Loop
accessibility: This trail traverses steep, rocky, and uneven terrain. Service animals permitted.
short_description: This .25 mile to 1.5 mile trail offers beautiful views of Rush Valley and gives hikers an understanding of the historic, mining, landscape. In the 1880s, zinc ore was discovered in the hills and claims were staked out along Rush Valley and neighboring Clabber Creek. Eventually, a community of homes and businesses developed along Rush Creek and endured until the 1960s. Come and explore this unique history as you hike Rush Mountain.

title: Hike the Indian Rockhouse Trail
accessibility: This is a narrow trail that traverses steep, uneven, and rocky terrain. Documented service animals are permitted.
short_description: A hike on the Indian Rockhouse reveals geologic formations commonly found on a limestone landscape and gives hikers an opportunity to explore locations where ancient peoples sought shelter.

title: Hōlei Sea Arch
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: The first portion of the walk is along a paved road, but the path immediately preceding the observation area is over rough, uneven lava rock
short_description: Walk a short distance to a view of dramatic sea cliffs and a 90-foot high arch sculpted by the sea.

title: Haʻakulamanu via Sulphur Banks Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: A wheelchair accessible trail to the Sulphur Banks area is located across the street from the Steam Vents parking lot.
short_description: See where volcanic gases have deposited colorful crystals.

title: Kūpinaʻi Pali (Waldron Ledge)
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Wheelchair and stroller accessible, though some sections of trail have a steep grade and may have cracks. The first small overlook past the Volcano House on the right has a very steep descent, but the larger overlook is wheelchair accessible.
short_description: Walk along an old road damaged by an earthquake in 1983 and get panoramic views of Kaluapele

title: Devastation Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Wheelchair and stroller accessible, though there are sections of this paved trail that have grades greater than eight percent (8%).
short_description: Stroll on a paved path through a recovering landscape that was buried by falling cinder from the 1959 Kīlauea Iki eruption.

title: Keanakākoʻi
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
short_description: Walk along an old portion of Crater Rim Drive to Keanakāko'i Crater and views toward the massive Halemaʻumaʻu.

title: Footprints Area
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Sections of trail are paved, but with steep inclines and occasional deep sand and uneven surfaces.
short_description: Traverse the rugged Kaʻū Desert and see footprints left by Native Hawaiians long ago.

title: Puʻuloa Petroglyphs Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fees apply. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Trail is over uneven, solidified lava fields
short_description: Hike across a lava field to the largest group of petroglyphs in Hawaiʻi.

title: Maunaulu via Nāpau Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Rough and uneven terrain with steep incline up Puʻuhuluhulu cinder cone.
short_description: Explore the 1969-1974 lava flows of Maunaulu and hike to the top of Puʻuhuluhulu cinder cone.

title: Nāhuku Lava Tube Trail
topics: Caves, Caverns and Karst;Rainforest;Scenic Views;Trails;Unique Species;Volcanoes
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Trail in and out of the lava tube is steep, and often slippery. There are also low ceilings, standing water, and tripping hazards
short_description: Walk through lush rainforest and see a cave where a river of lava flowed 500 years ago.

title: Visit Kahuku: Forested Pit Crater
topics: Meadows;Pacific Islander Heritage;Scenic Views;The Tropics;Trails;Unique Species;Endangered;Rare;Volcanoes
accessibility: Trail is on uneven grassy terrain, with significant elevation gain
short_description: Take a strenuous hike to a pit crater filled with an array of native Hawaiian species.

title: Visit Kahuku: Kona Trail
accessibility: Trail is on uneven grassy terrain, with significant elevation gain.
short_description: Hike through scenic pasturelands with native trees, and transverse the 1887 lava flow.

title: Visit Kahuku: Kamakapaʻa Trail
accessibility: Uneven trail through a grassy area with a steep gain in elevation
short_description: A walk up to a small cinder cone surrounded by rolling, grassy meadows

title: Visit Kahuku: Glover Trail
accessibility: Trail is on uneven grassy terrain, with significant elevation gain.
short_description: Take a strenuous hike to a pit crater filled with an array of native Hawaiian species.

title: Visit Kahuku: Puʻu o Lokuana
accessibility: Very steep elevation gain and uneven, grassy and rocky terrain
short_description: Hike to the top of Puʻu o Lokuana cinder cone, with choices for a shorter or longer loop.

title: Visit Kahuku: Palm Trail
accessibility: Trail is on uneven rock and grass, with significant hills and slope
short_description: Hike or bike to some of the best views of Kahuku and along the fissure of the 1868 Mauna Loa eruption

title: Kīlauea Iki Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Moderate to challenging trail. Steep and rocky with a 400' descent and ascent.
short_description: Descend 400 feet (122 m) through rainforest into a volcanic crater and hike across a hardened lava lake from the 1959 eruption.

title: Birdwatching at Kīpukapuaulu
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: The trail is a narrow dirt path with gentle inclines and declines. Note: dogs, horses and bicycles are prohibited on this trail.
short_description: Look for birds in a unique area of biological diversity with rare and endangered species.

title: Kīpukapuaulu Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: The trail is a narrow dirt path with gentle inclines and declines. Note: dogs, horses and bicycles are prohibited on this trail.
short_description: A loop hike through a unique area of biological diversity with rare plants, birds, and old-growth trees.

title: Halemaʻumaʻu Trail
accessibility: Trail is steep, uneven and occasionally narrow, descending nearly 425 feet (130m).
short_description: Hike down to the floor of Kaluapele (Kīlauea caldera), with possible longer connections to Byron Ledge, Kīlauea Iki, and Nāhuku.

title: Crater Rim Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee applies. There are no additional activity fees.
accessibility: Portions of Crater Rim Trail are paved, but much of it is on gravel or uneven surfaces with occasional steep inclines or stairs
short_description: Catch views of Kīlauea caldera, feel the breath of the volcano at Steaming Bluff (Wahinekapu), and walk through lush rainforest.

title: Visit the White River Visitor Center
topics: Bison;Horses (wild);Fossils and Paleontology;Geology;Grasslands;Prairies;US Air Force (Army Air Corps);Native American Heritage;Natural Sounds;Night Sky;Religion and Spirituality;Rock Landscapes and Features;Buttes;Scenic Views;Massacres;Westward Expansion;Homesteading;Wilderness
accessibility: The White River Visitor Center includes ramp entrances and spacious museum exhibits for those who use wheelchairs. Ask rangers at the front desk about audio-described and text-only brochures . Certified service animals are the only animals allowed in the visitor center. Emotional support animals are not service animals and are not allowed in the building.
short_description: The White River Visitor Center is the main facility in the South Unit of the park. Be sure to stop by to pick up maps, enjoy museum exhibits, and chat with rangers about the significance of the Badlands and treaties in Lakota heritage.

title: Day Trip or Backpack Hike to Coyote Gulch
topics: Canyons and Canyonlands;Geology;Freshwater Springs;Natural Sounds;Night Sky;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Arches;Buttes;Scenic Views
fee_description: Hiking and overnight permits are free, but make sure you get yours before you start hiking!
accessibility: Coyote Gulch is not recommended to people with low mobility. The road to access any of the trailheads is rough dirt and does not have accessible parking. The route is along an unpaved riverbed. Along the route, one may encounter deep sand, slickrock, wet slickrock, sheer cliffs that may require some technical gear, and water.
short_description: Open year-round but most popular in Spring and Fall, Coyote Gulch is a tributary of the Escalante River with several entry points for day hiking or backpacking in the Escalante Canyons of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area and Grand Staircase National Monument. This is a wilderness area, prepare to pack out everything you bring in.

title: Guided Cave Tours
fee_description: There are no entrance fees to the monument; however, there is an activity fee charged for each participant on the guided cave tours. More information can be found on our Fees & Passes page.
accessibility: The Discovery Talk is wheelchair accessible and service animal friendly. There are no stairs required on this tour. The smaller group size allows visitors to interact with the ranger more directly and have a more personalized experience. A wheelchair is available in the Visitor Center for visitors to use on the Discovery Talk if needed.
short_description: Ranger-guided tours are required to enter Jewel Cave, and the various tours are offered at scheduled times, which vary by season. With four different tour options, there is something for all skill levels and interests.

title: Climb the Saratoga Monument
topics: American Revolution;Architecture and Building;Military;Monuments and Memorials;Scenic Views;Wars and Conflicts;American Revolutionary War
accessibility: Restrooms: two partially accessible outdoor restrooms are available in the parking area on site - the stalls are wide enough, but doors into the restrooms are not automatic. Parking: two spaces available Walkway: a winding, paved path makes its way up a hill to the base of the Saratoga Monument Monument: four sets of four steps (one set of stairs on each side of the obelisk) lead to the lobby of the Saratoga Monument. An interpretive binder complete with information about the Monument's history and pictures of views is available for those unable to navigate the steps.
short_description: This 155-foot stone obelisk was built in the last quarter of the 19th century to commemorate the American victory in the Battles of Saratoga. Visitors may climb up its 188 steps to take in amazing views of the surrounding area, with up to 30+ mile visibility on clear days.

title: Visit the Roosevelt Gravesite at Youngs Memorial Cemetery
accessibility: A steep paved path leads most of the way to the Roosevelt gravesite. Visitors must then climb a 26 short steps to walk to the grave enclosure.
short_description: Youngs Memorial Cemetery is a small cemetery in the village of Oyster Bay, New York. Theodore Roosevelt, the twenty-sixth President of the United States, his wife Edith Roosevelt, and other Roosevelt family members are buried at Youngs Cemetery. It is located approximately one and a half miles south of Sagamore Hill National Historic Site.

title: Visit the White Haven Estate
accessibility: There is an accessible entrance into White Haven on the eastern side of the home, roughly 100 yards from the Visitor Center. All but one room on the main floor of the house is wheelchair accessible. The historic Winter Kitchen in the basement of the house can only be accessed by stairs. Park staff can provide a binder with photographs and interpretive text from the winter kitchen upon request. All outbuildings are accessible. A short film presentation in the historic dining room has closed captions and features an induction loop for visitors with T-coil enabled hearing aids. Learn more about accessibility at Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site.
short_description: Visit the historic White Haven estate.

title: Hike to Burroughs Mountain
fee_description: Park entrance fee required
accessibility: Burroughs Mountain Trail allows hikers to choose a shorter or longer hike depending on their fitness and preference. Getting to First Burroughs requires hiking uphill on a narrow, rocky trail with areas of steep drop offs. Continuing to Second Burroughs adds 250 feet elevation gain. Due to its high elevation, portions of the Burroughs Mountain trail can remain snow-covered after the road to Sunrise opens. Given the trail’s steep drop offs the presence of snow can make it more hazardous. Check trail conditions before hiking early in the season.
short_description: Hike the Burroughs Mountain Trail for outstanding mountain views and to visit the most accessible tundra in the Cascade Range.

title: Junior Ranger Activity Book
accessibility: Service animals are allowed inside the visitor center. A wheelchair is available for use - ask at the visitor center front desk. The visitor center has an accessible entrance on the west side of the building (2nd Street)
short_description: The Junior Ranger program is a great way to learn more about President William Jefferson Clinton Birthplace Home National Historic Site. Anyone can become a Junior Ranger by completing activities either during a visit to the park or by mail.

title: Drive East Portal Road
topics: Dams;Geology;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Trails;Roads, Routes and Highways;Tunnels
accessibility: East Portal Road is an accessible way to take in the scenic views of Black Canyon and Gunnison River. Parking areas are gravel and there is one wheelchair accessible vault toilet.
short_description: East Portal Road is a windy, steep scenic road down to the Gunnison River. East Portal is within Curecanti National Recreation Area, but only accessible from within Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park. Vehicles over 22 feet are prohibited on the East Portal Road.

title: Swim Lake Wood
accessibility: Lake Wood is not accessible. There is a short trail (.1 mi) connecting the small beach to the parking area. The trail has uneven footing and roots across it in areas. There are also no accessible restrooms at Lake Wood.
short_description: Lake Wood is a secluded pond with a small beach area, just a short drive away from Hulls Cove Visitor Center. There are no lifeguards and access road does not open until June 1.

title: Swim Sand Beach
accessibility: Sand Beach is not accessible. There is a large staircase leading down to the beach from the parking lot.
short_description: Acadia’s only sandy ocean beach, at the beginning of the Park Loop Road’s coastal section, is one of the park’s most heavily-visited areas. Visitors come to swim in the frigid water, bask and play on the sand, seek intertidal creatures, or view a feature widely publicized as a “must-see.”

title: Swim Echo Lake Beach
fee_description: Although this activity is free, a park entrance pass is required for all areas of the park from May 1 through October 31.
accessibility: Echo Lake Beach is accessible via a paved path from the parking lot to a connector boardwalk onto the beach. The restrooms are wheelchair-accessible.
short_description: Echo Lake Beach is a popular, freshwater swimming area on the southern end of Echo Lake. It is accessible off Route 102 in Southwest Harbor.

title: Hike Hermits Rest Trail
accessibility: This trail has uneven terrain, steep decents, and is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: Zigzagging through oak, pine, juniper, and fir, hikers descend more than 1750 ft (531 m) to a wooded camp and picnic sites on the shores of Morrow Point Reservoir.

title: Explore the Shiloh Visitor Center Museum
accessibility: The building is wheelchair accessible. Wheelchairs are available for loan, please notify a park ranger or park volunteer. Video diplays are closed captioned.
short_description: Visit Shiloh's museum exhibits in the park's visitor center.

title: Old North Church: Bell Ringing Chamber Tour
topics: American Revolution;Architecture and Building;Churches;American Revolutionary War
fee_description: Tickets: $10 per person (includes general admission to the sanctuary). Children 5 and under are free.
accessibility: Visitors must climb two sets of steep stairs for this tour.
short_description: Take a tour of Old North's bell tower! Visitors will explore the archive room and the bell ringing chamber: two behind-the-scenes areas that aren’t typically open to guests.

title: Tour the North Rim Road
topics: Canyons and Canyonlands;Forests and Woodlands;Geology;Mountains;Night Sky;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Scenic Views;Roads, Routes and Highways;Wilderness
accessibility: The North Rim Road is an accessible way to take in the scenic views along the canyon rim. There are no accessible or paved overlooks.
short_description: The North Rim is reached by taking a gravel road from the east end of Crawford State Park. The North Rim Road provides access to 6 overlooks. The canyon walls on the North Rim are almost vertical, offering impressive views.

title: Walk the River Loop Trail
topics: Forts;Military;US Army;Native American Heritage;River and Riparian;Scenic Views;Trails;Civil War;Tribal Conflicts
fee_description: No fees apply.
accessibility: Length: 1 mile Slope: Undulating with segments of 5% - 7%; steepest is 11% for 35 feet on the levee embankment. Cross slope: max 1% Surface material: Concrete Width: 5 feet There are multiple benches along the trail and interpretive waysides that can be viewed without blocking the sidewalk. The trail also crosses three active railroad tracks. Be alert for trains and the crossing are can be slippery and a possible trip hazard. No access to the river. No water or restrooms are located along the trail.
short_description: The trail is open year round. No access to the river. No water or restrooms are located along the trail.

title: Tenement Museum Tours
topics: African American Heritage;American Revolution;Architecture and Building;Asian American Heritage;Colonization and Settlement;Commerce;Enslavement;Great Depression;Hispanic American Heritage;Immigration;Industry;Factories;Mills;LGB American Heritage;Laborer and Worker;Labor Movement;Latino American Heritage;Medicine;Migrations;Native American Heritage;Pacific Islander Heritage;Religion and Spirituality;Schools and Education;Social Movements;Abolition Movement;Civil Rights;Conservation Movement;Religious Freedom;Voting Rights and Suffrage;Transportation;Urban America;Wars and Conflicts;Civil War;Cold War;Colonial/European Contact Conflicts;Korean War;Mexican War;Spanish-American War;Vietnam War;War of 1812;World War I;World War II
fee_description: The Tenement Museum Does Not Accept NPS Passes As an affiliated National Park Service site the Lower East Side Tenement Museum does not accept or sell National Park Passes, or any of the America the Beautiful—the National Parks and Federal Recreational Lands Passes.The Museum is only accessible by guided tenement apartment tours or neighborhood walking tours and requires the purchase of the appropriate ticket. Tickets are required for all tours. Apartment and Walking Tours Adults: $30 Seniors: $30 Students: $30 Museum Members: Free Food Experiences Adults: $55 Seniors:$55 Students:$55 Children under 5: Free Members: $27.50 (50% off) Online and phone orders are subject to a $2.00 per ticket service fee. The Museum also offers discounts for teachers, active military, neighborhood residents (10002 zip code), visitors with disabilities, and members of AAM, MANY, and National Trust. Discounted tickets purchased online or through phone orders are still subject to service fees. For more information, email us at LESTM@tenement.org
accessibility: Accessibility Information The Tenement Museum welcomes all visitors. We recognize the diverse needs of our audience and offer accessible programs and services to enable all visitors to explore the stories we interpret at the Tenement Museum. For questions about Museum accessibility and how we can accommodate your specific needs, contact our Visitor Services team by calling (877) 975-3786 or e-mailing LESTM@tenement.org . Membership The Tenement Museum offers a special $65 membership for visitors with disabilities.For more information, please call our Membership Office at (646) 518-3007. Free entry to care partners Regardless of Museum membership status, all visitors with disabilities can obtain free entry for their care partners upon request. Service Animal Policy Service dogs are welcome on all museum tours. However, pets and emotional support animals are not allowed inside tenement buildings, but can be brought on outdoor neighborhood walking tours. Wheelchair Accessibility The following tours are wheelchair accessible: Finding Home Reclaiming Black Spaces Building on the Lower East Side Outside the Home The Museum has a limited amount of wheelchairs available to borrow for wheelchair accessible programs. To reserve a wheelchair for your visit, please contact our Call Center at 877-975-3786 (Monday–Saturday: 9 am–5 pm) or e-mail LESTM@tenement.org Individuals who are Blind or have Low Vision Handling objects are available for our 100 Years Apart, Finding Home , and Tenement Women:1902 tours. Ask for these materials when you arrive at the Visitors Center. Visitors can book a free tactile orientation to the Museum before their tour with two weeks’ advance notice. Individuals who are Deaf or have Hearing Loss Assistive Listening Devices Assistive listening devices are available on all tours. However, these devices are not compatible with most hearing aids. For visitors who cannot use an assisted listening device, we can provide simultaneous transcription of the tour on an iPad with at least 24 hours notice. The Museum can also arrange ASL interpretation of a tour with at least 2 weeks notice. To request simultaneous transcription service or book an ASL interpreter through the Museum, please call or email us. Language Aids The Museum offers simultaneous translation aid on our tenement apartment tours using the Forum app. Please note that translation will be limited during parts of our A Union of Hope: 1869, Family Owned, and 100 Years Apart tours due to interactive technical components. If you are interested in using a translation aid during your visit, please email us for options.
short_description: The guided tours currently offered by the Lower East Side Tenement Museum.

title: Watch the Sunrise from Pounding Mill Overlook
accessibility: Large, paved overlook on the Blue Ridge Parkway. Views can be seen from inside or outside of a vehicle. There are no facilities at this overlook.
short_description: Sunrise on the Blue Ridge Parkway can be an amazing, once-in-a-lifetime experience. Pounding Mill Overlook at Milepost 413 is a great place to welcome the dawn of a new day and appreciate the natural beauty of this special place.

title: Go Fishing in the Cuyahoga Valley
accessibility: Kendall Lake and Horseshoe Pond offer fully accessible fishing experiences with paved paths from the parking lots to the docks. Distances from parking lots to ponds vary from less than 100 yards to 3/4 mile.
short_description: Fishing is a great way to spend your day in Cuyahoga Valley National Park. Learn about the best places to fish and how to responsibly enjoy this pastime.

title: Backcountry Camping
accessibility: The backcountry of Badlands National Park often includes rough terrain and is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: Backcountry camping in the Badlands can be an exciting adventure for prepared and experienced hikers. Read more about rules, safety, and recommendations for backcountry campers here.

title: Hike to Blue Hen Falls from Boston
accessibility: This section of the Buckeye Trail is not wheelchair accessible. It is hilly with an unpaved surface that is rocky and muddy in places. There are multiple staircases along this hike. Service animals and leashed comfort pets are welcome. Audio description is available for exhibit panels in the visitor center.
short_description: Blue Hen Falls is a popular hike-in destination in the Boston area. Hikers can reach the waterfall via the Buckeye Trail from Boston Mill Visitor Center. Learn more about this popular hilly hike.

title: Drive U.S. Highway 50
topics: Canyons and Canyonlands;Dams;Plateaus and Mesas;Geology;Lakes;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Scenic Views;Roads, Routes and Highways;Trains and Railroads
accessibility: U.S. Highway 50 is a paved state highway. There are multiple wheelchair accessible restrooms along the way.
short_description: U.S. Highway 50 travels west from Gunnison and brings you into Curecanti National Recreation Area. The highway follows along the Gunnison River before reaching Blue Mesa Reservoir, continuing along its edge and crossing two bridges.

title: Drive CO Highway 92
topics: Canyons and Canyonlands;Dams;Plateaus and Mesas;Geology;Lakes;Mountains;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Scenic Views;Transportation;Roads, Routes and Highways
accessibility: CO Highway 92 is a paved state highway. There are wheelchair accessible restrooms along the way.
short_description: Colorado (CO) Highway 92 crosses over Blue Mesa Dam and winds along the north rim of the Black Canyon, providing access to scenic overlooks and trailheads.

title: Crescent Meadow Wildlife
accessibility: A limited number of accessible but steep parking spaces are available at the trailhead near the restrooms. This small parking area often fills up. In the summer, free shuttles run from Giant Forest Museum to the Crescent Meadow parking area. On weekends, the road closes to private vehicles and shuttles are the only way to reach Moro Rock and Crescent Meadow. On weekdays, the road remains open, but the small parking area may be full. The trail is partially paved and may be accessible, depending on abilities.
short_description: Keep your eyes and ears open for wildlife as you hike along the Crescent Meadow in trail Sequoia's Giant Forest.

title: Tokopah Falls Wildlife
accessibility: There is no parking at the trailhead. Parking is located next to the Lodgepole Campground in the overflow lot. This parking area is paved, and has accessible parking spaces near the restrooms. The trailhead is a short distance from the parking area on a paved road. The trail is unpaved dirt, and contains uneven and rocky terrain.
short_description: Keep your eyes and ears open for wildlife as you hike along the Tokopah Falls trail.

title: Picnic at Willow Beach
fee_description: The Willow Beach Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Willow Beach picnic area features 9 picnic tables, 5 grills, restrooms, and drinking water.

title: Picnic at Las Vegas Bay
fee_description: The Las Vegas Bay Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Las Vegas Bay picnic area features 18 picnic tables, 8 grills, restrooms, and drinking water.

title: Picnic at Callville Bay
fee_description: The Callville Bay Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Callville Bay picnic area features 8 picnic tables, 8 grills, restrooms, and drinking water.

title: Picnic at Blue Point Spring
fee_description: The Blue Point Spring Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Blue Point Spring picnic area features 1 picnic table with mountainous landscape views. There are no restrooms, drinking water, or grills.

title: Picnic at 33 Hole Overlook
fee_description: The 33 Hole Overlook Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Enjoy a picnic with panoramic views of the Las Vegas Bay and the Black Mesa. 33 Hole Overlook Picnic area features 9 picnic tables, 9 grills, and restrooms. This location does not have drinking water.

title: Picnic at Boulder Beach
fee_description: The Boulder Beach Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Enjoy a picnic while looking out at Boulder Basin and Fortification Hill. Boulder Beach Picnic Area features 54 picnic tables, 18 grills, restrooms and drinking water.

title: Picnic at Longview Overlook
fee_description: The Longview Overlook Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Longview Picnic Area is a great spot to stop and have a picnic at along Lakeshore Road. This picnic area features 3 picnic tables, 3 grills, and restrooms. This location does not have drinking water.

title: Picnic at Redstone
fee_description: The Redstone Picnic Area is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: N/A
short_description: Redstone Picnic Area is nestled in the Pinto Valley Wilderness, along Northshore Road. Redstone picnic area features 3 picnic tables, 3 grills, and restrooms. This location does not have drinking water.

title: Join a Ranger Program
accessibility: Pets are not allowed at ranger programs, but service animals are welcome. Geology programs are offered at accessible overlooks. Campground evening programs can be accessed by a ramp; wheelchairs require assistance due to steepness.
short_description: Ranger program offerings vary throughout the year. Stop by the South Rim Visitor Center for current offerings and times.

title: Bike the Historic Railroad Tunnel Trail
fee_description: The Historical Railroad Tunnel Trail is in a fee area, like the rest of the park. Keep your park pass or proof of admission with your vehicle for rangers to inspect.
accessibility: This trail is considered accessible.
short_description: The Historic Railroad Tunnel Trail features incredible vistas of Lake Mead and Boulder Basin and five tunnels – each approximately 25 feet wide.

title: Stargazing on Cadillac Mountain (Vehicle Access Limited)
fee_description: Although the activity is free, a park entrance pass is required for all areas of the park. During the daytime, advance reservations are required to drive up Cadillac Mountain and there is no overnight parking. Vehicular access to Cadillac Summit is subject to night closures so check out our Current Conditions page for up to date information. You do not need reservations to hike or bike to the summit; always bring flashlights or bike lights for night excursions.
accessibility: The parking lots and portions of Cadillac Summit Loop are accessible. Extra caution is required after dark. There is an accessible restroom at the summit.
short_description: Gaze in awe at Acadia's night sky from the highest mountain summit in the park.

title: Hike Crystal Creek Trail
accessibility: This trail has significant elevation change and is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: Winding through abundant wildflowers, Gambel oak, aspens, conifers and a recovering burn area, Crystal Creek Trail is ideal for spring or fall hiking.

title: Paddle the East Branch of the Penobscot River (From Lunksoos Boat Launch to Big Seboeis)
fee_description: Paddlers must prepare their own equipment and transportation for this activity.
accessibility: Both the landing at Lunksoos Boat Launch and at Big Seboeis Campsite are unpaved. There are no services available at these areas. The landings are both a mixture of dirt and gravel that slope down into the water. The ground may be slick and/or uneven. The inclines of both boat launch landings may exceed accessibility standards for wheelchair use. There is an accessible restroom at the Lunksoos Boat Launch.
short_description: Enjoy paddling the East Branch of the Penobscot River in Katahdin Woods and Waters!

title: Level 1 Trails at Fort Vancouver National Historic Site
accessibility: Level 1 trails are wheelchair accessible. Access to the Columbia River waterfront/beach area is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: Learn about Level 1 walking trails at Fort Vancouver. Level 1 trails are wheelchair-accessible and can be walked in 15 minutes with minimal elevation change.

title: Level 2 Trails at Fort Vancouver National Historic Site
accessibility: Level 2 trails are wheelchair accessible. Please use caution on areas of the Land Bridge Trail, which can be slippery when wet.
short_description: Learn about Level 2 walking trails at Fort Vancouver. Level 2 trails are wheelchair-accessible and can be walked in under 30 minutes with an elevation change of less than 20 feet.

title: Level 3 Trails at Fort Vancouver National Historic Site
accessibility: The Lower River Road trail is not wheelchair accessible, and crosses areas covered by grass and gravel. The Parade Ground and East Vancouver Barracks loop trails are not fully wheelchair-accessible. Both routes cross 300 feet of uneven grass. The Great Meadow trail follows 300 feet of road shoulder.
short_description: Learn about Level 3 walking trails at Fort Vancouver. Level 3 trails and routes can be walked in 90 minutes with an elevation change of up to 50 feet.

title: Become a Tumacácori Junior Ranger
topics: Animals;Architecture and Building;Colonization and Settlement;Farming and Agriculture;Hispanic American Heritage;Latino American Heritage;Native American Heritage;Missions;Colonial/European Contact Conflicts
fee_description: A donation to support printing costs is much appreciated.
accessibility: All Junior Ranger activities can take place along the paved trails and other accessible locations within the mission grounds.
short_description: The complex narrative of Tumacácori doesn't have to be dry or confusing. You just need the right feathered guide! Pancho the Vermilion Flycatcher will guide young Junior Rangers through the park. Older children explore the park following a visual treasure hunt.

title: Earn Your Cabrillo Junior Ranger Badge
fee_description: No additional fee. Entrance fees for the park may apply.
accessibility: The Cabrillo Junior Ranger book is designed to be accessible for people of all ages and cognitive abilities. There are no age requirements for the activities. Children, especially those younger than 5 years old, may need assistance from parents or guradians with activities.
short_description: How to earn your Cabrillo National Monument Junior Ranger badge

title: Hike Chasm View Nature Trail - North Rim
accessibility: This unpaved trail is rocky in places and not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: This short loop trail breaks out of the pinyon/juniper forest at the North Chasm View to provide excellent views of Painted Wall and Serpent Point.

title: Hike Cedar Point Nature Trail - South Rim
accessibility: This trail is unpaved and not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: This short, moderately sloped trail offers visitors a chance to brush up on local flora with guideposts describing the various plants along the way.

title: Hike Oak Flat Trail - South Rim
accessibility: This trail is unpaved, steep, and not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: This 1.6 mi (2.6 km) trail offers variety to the hiker who would like to explore below the rim without going all the way to the river. The trail is narrow in places and traverses some steep slopes.

title: Hike Warner Point Trail - South Rim
accessibility: This unpaved trail is steep in places and not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: Warner Point Trail provides views of various mountain ranges, the Black Canyon, and the Gunnison River. Nature trail guides are available at High Point Overlook or the South Rim Visitor Center.

title: Picnic at the Katahdin Loop Road Overlook
accessibility: The Katahdin Loop Road Overlook has a vault toilet and several picnic tables. There is a step up to use the vault toilet. Vehicles will park in a dirt and gravel parking area. The ground surface of the overlook may be uneven with rocks, grass, and gravel.
short_description: Enjoy a beautiful expansive view of Katahdin and the region from the Katahdin Loop Road Overlook.

title: Wayside Loop Trail
accessibility: The trail varies between a dirt/gravel carriage road around Van Buren's home and grass/dirt when heading out towards the farm fields. Service Animals are allowed on all parts of the trail.
short_description: The Wayside Loop Trail is a short tour of the site that visitors can do at any time.

title: Birding on the Natchez Trace Parkway
accessibility: Birding can be enjoyed by anyone, anywhere, even from the comfort of your vehicle. Most trails along the Parkway are not accessible. For more information, please see our accessibility page: Accessibility - Natchez Trace Parkway (U.S. National Park Service) (nps.gov)
short_description: Birding on the Natchez Trace Parkway

title: Visit the Lodgepole Visitor Center
fee_description: (subject to park entrance fees).
accessibility: The visitor center is typically open May through mid-October. The entrance to the visitor center has a low-energy, power-operated door with two push buttons, one at wheelchair height and another within a kick zone. The visitor center’s interior has barrier-free access to interpretive exhibits, the park store, and a standing-height ranger desk. Audio description and assistive listening devices are available upon request for park films. Outside the visitor center, there are dual-height drinking fountains with a water bottle filling station and a lowered pay phone. Accessible restrooms are available around the side of the building. Soundscapes Exhibit: At Lodgepole Visitor Center, immerse yourself in the diverse soundscapes of each altitudinal zone of the parks as you travel through the exhibits. From the grassy foothills all the way up to the high mountains, hear birdsong, bears, pika, and even inside Crystal Cave. This accessible exhibit features high-quality audio that is motion-triggered as you move through the rooms.
short_description: With brand new museum exhibits, a Park Store, and a wilderness information counter, the Lodgepole Visitor Center is the place to be.

title: Hike the Wuksachi Trail
accessibility: There is a larged paved parking lot at the trailhead. There are no designated accessible parking spaces. The trail is unpaved dirt with uneven rocky terrain.
short_description: Head out on the Wuksachi Trail to Lodgepole for a walk through fir forests, meadows, and creeks. Venture into the wilderness by connecting to the Twin Lakes Trail for Cahoon Meadow, or continue to Lodgepole, where you can catch the Purple Route 2 shuttle back to Wuksachi Lodge (summer only).

title: Bike Redwoods to Beach on the Ossagon Trail Loop
topics: Forests and Woodlands;Meadows;Logging and Timber Cutting;Natural Sounds;Oceans;Scenic Views;Trails;Unique Species;Endangered
accessibility: These trails are not wheelchair accessible due to steep grades, uneven surfaces, and narrow path width.
short_description: Follow a 19-mile loop through old-growth redwood forests to the Pacific coast and back. The route combines Ossagon Trail, Coastal Trail (Gold Beach Section), Davison Road and Newton B. Drury Scenic Parkway.

title: Hike Among the Giants
accessibility: Congress Trail is a 2.7 mile round-trip lollipop-shaped trail on a gentle, paved incline. It begins near the General Sherman Tree, the largest living tree on Earth. For accessible access to the Congress Trail and General Sherman Tree, park at the small parking area along the Generals Highway two miles (3.2 km) north of the Giant Forest Museum. Parking in this lot is designated accessible only. If you do not have a placard, but cannot manage a steep slope or stairs on the main trail to the Sherman Tree, stop at a visitor center for a temporary pass. In summer, if parking here is unavailable, park instead at Lodgepole Visitor Center, Giant Forest Museum, or General Sherman Tree Main Trail and Parking and take the wheelchair accessible park shuttle (Green Route 1). From here, the trail to the General Sherman Tree is paved with inclines of up to 5% and limited cross-slopes. There are benches along the trail.
short_description: There is no better way to explore the Giant Forest than by going out on the trails. Try a stroll on the Congress Trail, a 2-mile (3.2-km) loop that starts from the General Sherman Tree and takes you into the heart of a sequoia grove.

title: Explore the Winter Forest by Foot
fee_description: Snowshoes are available for rent at Lodgepole Market or Wuksachi Lodge .
accessibility: Accessible-only parking lots are available next to the Giant Forest Museum and at the Big Trees Trailhead. General parking is available across the street from the Giant Forest Museum. In the winter expect icy parking lots, and snow-covered trails.
short_description: There is no better way to see the snow covered Giant Forest than to get out on the trails and walk around. Whether you rent snowshoes or bring your own, snowshoeing around a sequoia grove is a fun experience for people who are well-prepared.

title: Discover the Lodgepole-Sherman Tree Trail
accessibility: Parking is located at the Lodgepole Campground overflow parking lot. This parking area is paved, and has accessible parking spaces near the restrooms. The trail is unpaved dirt, and contains uneven and rocky terrain.
short_description: Explore the Giant Forest on your way to the General Sherman Tree. Take the 2.8 mile Lodgepole-Sherman Tree Trail from the Lodgepole Campground, then catch the Green Route 1 shuttle back to the parking lot.

title: Enjoy a 360-Degree View at Little Baldy Dome
accessibility: There is paved pullout parking on either side of the road, with no designated accessible parking spaces. The trail is a dirt path with uneven, rocky terrain.
short_description: Hike on a lesser-known trail in Sequoia National Park. The Little Baldy trail takes you through a mixed-conifer forest to the top of a granite dome. Once there, you can take in a 360-degree panoramic view.

title: Off Road Vehicles in Glen Canyon
topics: Canyons and Canyonlands;Rock Landscapes and Features;Scenic Views;Roads, Routes and Highways
fee_description: A permit system is in development. Once the permit system is in place, they will be required for the following areas. All Shoreline Access Areas Ferry Swale Area, including Corrals Road and Seismograph Road Lone Rock Beach and Lone Rock Play Area ORV Permits are separate from park entrance fees. To purchase a entrance pass, tap the fees icon in the black bar. Camping & ORVs There is no additional camping fee or permit required to camp in undeveloped backcountry areas, with some exceptions: Backcountry permits are required for all overnight stays in the Escalante District of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Obtain permits at the Escalante Interagency Visitor Center in the town of Escalante or at one of the entry trailheads. Day use does not require a backcountry permit, but please sign the trail register. Backcountry camping in the Orange Cliffs area of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area requires a permit from Canyonlands National Park.
accessibility: You must be able to drive or ride in a conventional vehicle, street-legal ATV, or off highway vehicle to participate in Off Road Diving. There are over 300 miles of roads available, all in various states of repair. Few roads are paved and have access to comfort facilities. Unpaved roads may or may not be passable in inclement weather. Shoreline Access Areas, when open, access the shoreline of Lake Powell, but there are no facilities available there. Getting out of your vehicle and walking around when Off Road Driving is optional. Service animals are permitted in the areas in Glen Canyon that are closed to pets.
short_description: Off-road vehicle use is allowed in the park only on National Park Service-designated ORV routes and areas, delineated by ORV route maps. Some Shoreline Access Areas indicated on the maps may not be available seasonally, due to changes in lake level. Note: There are 388 miles of Designated Roads of which 304 miles are unpaved.

title: Golf in DC's National Parks
fee_description: A full list of Greens Fees is available on the Play DC Golf website for the Rock Creek Park Golf Course .
accessibility: Information on accessibility is available on the Play DC Golf website
short_description: Visit one of three golf courses at National Parks in Washington, DC

title: View Sunset from Sunset Rock
topics: Forests and Woodlands;Rock Landscapes and Features;Scenic Views;Trails
accessibility: This is an unpaved dirt trail consisting of uneven terrain. There is no parking at the trailhead, but paved paths from various parking areas lead to it. Some paths contain rock steps. General parking is available across the street from the Giant Forest Museum, and is the closest to the trailhead. Accessible parking is available next to the Giant Forest Museum and at the Big Trees Trailhead.
short_description: Are you looking for the perfect spot for sunset? Head to Sunset Rock in the Giant Forest. This less trafficked trail is a great option for escaping the crowds and enjoying the colorful sunset.

title: Explore the FDR Presidential Library Exhibits
fee_description: Admission fees: Adults (ages 16 to 61): $15.00 Seniors (ages 62 and over): $10.00 Ages under 16: No admission fee.
accessibility: The Presedential Library is accessible. Video features throughout the exhibits are captioned.
short_description: The Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum is independently operated and maintained by the National Archives and Records Administration, a federal agency.

title: Big Bend Junior Rangers
topics: Animals;Birds;Canyons and Canyonlands;Plateaus and Mesas;Fossils and Paleontology;Natural Sounds;Night Sky;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Trails;Wilderness
accessibility: We are continually working to upgrade facilities for accessibility and to improve park access for all visitors. While not all facilities are fully accessible, park rangers are happy to assist any visitor with special needs. Some Junior Ranger activities are available on the park website.
short_description: Big Bend National Park invites young visitors to become official Junior Rangers.

title: Visit the William Johnson House
accessibility: The William Johnson House is accessible
short_description: The William Johnson House offers visitors the opportunity to connect with a free man of color and his family during the antebellum era.

title: Hunting In The Seboeis Parcel
season: Refer to the Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife season dates and bag limit laws and rules.
accessibility: This area is very undeveloped. The Seboeis Parcel is brushy with uneven terrain. Trails and roads are uneven with gravel, rocks, and dirt. Depending on the season there may be deep mud. There is currently no accessible parking areas or toilets in the Seboeis Parcel.
short_description: Learn about hunting in the Seboeis Parcel of Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument.

title: Hike the Capers Creek Trail
accessibility: The Capers Creek trail is an easy 0.25 mile one way trail. The trail starts at the end of the grass field behind Darrah Hall. There is no wheelchair accessible path to the trail. There are roots on the path of the trail.
short_description: Walk in the footsteps of Martin Luther King Jr. and the students of the Penn School on the Capers Creek Trail. This 0.25 mile trail through the woods of Saint Helena Island leads to a sweeping view of the marshes.

title: View Wildlife
fee_description: Park admission provides access to this activity.
accessibility: Viewpoints provide paved, flat surfaces accessible to all. Trails will vary. Visit our Accessibility page for more information.
short_description: The canyons and plateau of Bryce Canyon National Park are home to many animals. Park boundaries mean little to the migratory hummingbirds, nesting Peregrine Falcon, Rocky Mountain Elk and Pronghorn which daily cross through the forested plateau and amphitheaters. The search for food and water leads them to the best place to find sustenance and shelter. Many animals share habitats. Ebb and flow of populations is interdependent on all the members of the wildlife community.

title: Finding a Sense of Place at the Homestead
fee_description: There is no fee to tour the Homestead, but tickets are required. Tickets are available at the Visitor Center and must be obtained no later than 15 minutes prior to tour time.
accessibility: The Homestead may be accesible on the ground floors, with assistance. There is a video tour available at the Visitor Center.
short_description: When you cross the threshold on a guided tour of President Andrew Johnson’s Homestead, you are stepping into the past. The family’s 24-year home is filled with belongings original to their return home from Washington, D.C in 1869. Three subsequent generations of descendants inhabited the house, ensuring its preservation as a treasure trove of authentic family possessions and stories.

title: Rapids Bridge Hike
topics: Architecture and Building;Forests and Woodlands;Deciduous Forests;Geology;Natural Sounds;Rock Landscapes and Features;Trails;Bridges
accessibility: Rapids Bridge Hike uses the wide bridle trail known as the White Horse Trail for it's initial descent. This trail is 6-8 feet wide and is relatively smooth and free of obstructions. The trail continues along the edge of the creek to Rapids Bridge, which is roughly four feet wide and sixty feet across. The trail that returns to the nature center can narrow in width to four feet and is steep and can have hazards, such as exposed roots and rocks. For an accessible alternative, visitors can exit the Nature Center and make use of the paved multi-use trail that parallels Military Road to go to the creek. From there, Beach Drive is a paved alternative to get to Rapids Bridge. The ascent back to the Nature Center via the paved multi-use path is steep. Take your time and use caution. If you prefer not to make the descent and have to come back up the hill you can park your vehicle at Picnic Grove #6 to access Beach Drive. Beach Drive is closed to motor vehicle traffic on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays.
short_description: This 2-mile loop hike takes you through the forest and then parallels scenic Rock Creek before heading back uphill.

title: Boulder Bridge Hike
fee_description: Rock Creek Park is a fee free area.
accessibility: Trail starts at the Rock Creek Horse Center where it is roughly six feet across and relatively smooth, though there are occasional roots and rocks. The decent is sustained over half a mile. The bridle trail along the creek rises and falls with the natural terrain along the bank of the creek. The trail crosses Rapids Bridge which is a narrow concrete and metal bridge roughly four feet in width and forty feet across. The most accessible portion of this route is the segment that is on Beach Drive NW between Rapids Bridge and Boulder Bridge. The trail continues up a steep two foot wide foot trail. The ascent is steady and covers several hundred feet in elevation over half a mile. Visitors must once again cross a road stepping up and over curbs. The trail continues along the bridle trails though there are foot traffic only options. The foot traffic only option will be much more rugged and narrow while the bridle trails are wider and slightly smoother. A steep ascent up to another roadway and crossing curbs will bring visitors back to Picnic Grove #13 where additional roads and curbs will need to be crossed to return to the Nature Center.
short_description: Hike the 3.5-mile Boulder Bridge Loop from the Rock Creek Park Nature Center to one of the most iconic places in Rock Creek Park

title: Bark Ranger at hampton
accessibility: Pets are welcome on the grounds of Hampton, most of the grounds are accessible by gravel paths that cut through the property.
short_description: Learn about best practices for visiting Hampton NHS with pets.

title: Explore the Mesa Top Loop Road
topics: Archeology;Cliff Dwellings;Architecture and Building;Canyons and Canyonlands;Plateaus and Mesas;Native American Heritage;Scenic Views;Trails
accessibility: Moderate . A six-mile (10 km) loop road with a series of short trails to excavated archeological sites and spectacular cross-canyon views. You will find designated parking and restrooms mid-way along the road. Trail guide available. First Pithouse: Paved, level 50 foot (15 m) trail. Navajo Canyon Overlook: A flat, paved overlook adjacent to the parking area offers beautiful views of Navajo Canyon and Echo House cliff dwelling. Canyon views from your vehicle. Square Tower House Overlook: Paved, slightly sloping trail, about 200 yards (183 m) long. Spectacular birds-eye view of Square Tower House. Pithouses and Pueblos: Paved, level trails about 50 to 150 yards (46 to 137 m) long to three excavated sites. Mesa Top Sites: Paved, level 100 yard (91 m) trail with a 1% grade. Excavated site covered for weather protection. Sun Point Pueblo: Flat, paved 50 yard (46 m) easy trail to ancient pueblo, covered for weather protection. Sun Point View: Short walk leads to an uneven sandstone overlook with guardrails where you can see 12 alcove sites, including Cliff Palace. There are 12 tall, uneven stone steps on the left and about a 40 foot (12.2 m) ramp on the right. Oak Tree House Overlook: View this site from your vehicle if you wish. The overlook is uneven sandstone with guardrails. Parking is limited. Fire Temple and New Fire House Overlooks: View these sites from your vehicle if you wish. To get a closer view, there are three tall, uneven stone steps from the parking area to the sandstone viewpoint. Sun Temple: The best panoramic view of Cliff Palace can be seen here from your vehicle. Walk to Sun Temple on the paved, mostly level 200 yard (183 m) trail.
short_description: The 6-mile (10 km) Mesa Top Loop takes you through 700 years of Ancestral Pueblo history. From remains of early pithouses and masonry villages to multi-storied cliff dwellings, the archeological sites along this loop show how early Pueblo architecture evolved. Archeology and Pueblo oral histories shed light on what life may have been like for people who lived, worked, and raised families here for generations.

title: Bike Lost Man Creek Trail
topics: Colonization and Settlement;Forests and Woodlands;Coniferous Forests;Industry;Logging and Timber Cutting;Natural Sounds;Scenic Views;Trails;Unique Species;Rare;Westward Expansion
accessibility: Lost Man Trail is not wheelchair accessible due to steep grades and rough, uneven trail surfaces. The trailhead parking lot has accessible parking and an accessible restroom.
short_description: Lost Man Creek flows through a landscape greatly changed from the 1960s when much of this area was clearcut logged. What used to be a logging road has been converted into a hike and bike trail. Lost Man Creek trail is now a narrow single-track mountain-biking trail. The first couple of miles is in old-growth redwood groves.

title: Visit Forks of the Road
topics: African American Heritage;Enslavement;Abolition Movement;Tragic Events;Forced Marches;Civil War
accessibility: The site at Forks of the Road is relatively small and consists primarily of free-standing exhibits and wayside panels that are accessible. There is also an artistic depiction of slave manacles and chains in a concrete form. The entire site is accessible and easy to navigate. Most of the exhibits are located close to an adjacent sidewalk and some may be viewed from your car. Pets are welcome.
short_description: From 1833 to 1863, Forks of the Road was the second largest slave market in the Deep South. Tens of thousands of enslaved men, women and children were transported from Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky, and the Carolinas to the market at Natchez. The slave market operated from 1833 until the arrival of Federal troops on July 13, 1863.

title: Amache Self-Guided Driving Tour
accessibility: Requires driving on uneven, washed out gravel roads. There are not currently transcripts available for the tour. Check back soon for updates.
short_description: Amache Preservation Society has created a self-driving audio tour that leads visitors to 11 points of interest at the historic site.

title: Sagamore Hill Little Free Library
accessibility: The Little Free Library is located adjacent to the parking lot on a paved pea-gravel path.
short_description: Read like a Roosevelt! Take a book or leave a book at the Sagamore Hill Little Free Library.

title: Watch Peregrine Falcons at Devils Courthouse
accessibility: The best spot for viewing peregrine falcons at Devils Courthouse is from the overlook. It is a large paved parking area with a large grassy median that separates it from the Parkway. A level sidewalk with one step up separates the parking area from a narrow strip of grass and a sloping drop off to the forest below. Birdwatchers can stand in the parking area (if safe) or they can step up onto the sidewalk to watch the sky for birds soaring overhead. Do be careful of your footing. Many birdwatchers have learned that looking up and standing near a curb can be dangerous. Vehicles can be parked so that the viewer can see out over the expanse of the overlook to the sky beyond.
short_description: Peregrine falcon, once near extinction, now can be viewed in the skies over the Blue Ridge Parkway.

title: Hike to Haskell Rock
season: The North Gate may be closed during the late fall, winter, or early spring months. If you plan to visit during the time that the North Gate is closed, you will start the hike from the parking lot at North Gate. The total distance will be approximately 11 miles (round-trip) from the North Gate parking lot. Check the current conditions page before visiting the monument for most updated conditions.
accessibility: The trail surface is mostly dirt, gravel, and organic matter. It can be very muddy and slippery. Be careful of larger rocks on the trail and uneven terrain. The Haskell Rock viewing area is uneven and rocky with exposed roots. The elevation gain is 103ft / 31m.
short_description: Hike a total of 4 miles along the East Branch of the Penobscot River on the International Appalachian Trail to view Haskell Rock.

title: Become a Haleakalā Junior Ranger
accessibility: Digital activites online are accessible for visitors using screen readers.
short_description: Complete activities featuring the plants, animals, and history of Haleakalā to earn your Junior Ranger badge!

title: Become a Junior Ranger at Sunset Crater Volcano
fee_description: The booklet and badge are completely free. Regular park fees apply for visiting the monument.
accessibility: Activities are organized by engagement levels instead of age groups so Jr. Rangers of any age or ability can choose the activities that are best for them.
short_description: Explore Sunset Crater Volcano and learn about geology, wildlife, starry skies and how you can help us protect national parks.

title: Meet the Mules
topics: Horses (wild);Explorers and Expeditions;Farming and Agriculture;Immigration;Industry;Laborer and Worker;Labor Movement;Migrant Workers;Military;Presidents;Schools and Education;Water Trails;Transportation;Canals;Trains and Railroads;Westward Expansion
accessibility: The mule pen is accessible by a concrete and dirt path.
short_description: Interactive program with live mules.

title: Drive Park Boulevard
accessibility: Accessibility can vary greatly depending on where you would like to stop. The Oasis of Mara and Lower Keys View Overlook are two popular sites that are suitable for all types of wheelchairs. Learn more about planning a trip with physical mobility in mind , or talk to a ranger at a visitor center or entrance station for information on specific locations. Service animals are allowed but must be kept on a leash and all human food and waste rules apply to service animals as well. Learn more about service animals . Pets and emotional support animals are not allowed on trails.
short_description: A scenic drive through Joshua Tree National Park.

title: Hike the Estero Trail to Home Bay
accessibility: This trail traverses rolling terrain over short grass and packed dirt surfaces. With the exception of some ruts and animal holes, the trail surface is largely flat and even for the first 1.2 miles (1.9 km). The trailhead parking lot is dirt/gravel and the vault toilets do not meet accessibility standards.
short_description: This trail through grassland and an abandoned Christmas tree farm to the head of Home Bay offers the opportunity to see the birds, bat rays, and leopard sharks that call these habitats home. Allow 25 minutes driving time from Bear Valley to the Estero Trailhead.

title: Birding at Point Reyes National Seashore
accessibility: Outlooks, trails, and beaches vary in degree of accessibility. Contact the visitor center for more information on each specific area.
short_description: Point Reyes National Seashore offers some of the finest birding in the United States. About 54% of all North American bird species have been observed in Point Reyes National Seashore. Learn about where to look for birds and what kinds of birds you might find at the seashore.

title: Become a Point Reyes Junior Ranger!
accessibility: Check the park's accessibility guide (814 KB PDF) for more information on accessible areas in Point Reyes National Park. Not all areas suggested in the Junior Ranger booklet are accessible, but it gives users a variety of options and it isn't required that you visit all of them.
short_description: Do you care about exploring, learning about, and protecting Point Reyes National Seashore? If so, become a Junior Ranger!

title: Boating in the Backwaters
fee_description: Our boat ramp is free but boat and kayak rental will cost money if you do not bring your own.
accessibility: The City of Jacksonville has 3 adaptive kayak launches located at: Bethesda Park - 10790 Key Haven Boulevard, Jacksonville, FL 32218 , Kathryn Abbey Hanna Park - 500 Wonderwood Drive, Jacksonville, FL 32233 and Southbank Riverwalk - 1001 Museum Circle, Jacksonville, FL 32207 The Hanna Park launch is the nearest to Timucuan Preserve.
short_description: Sailboat, fishing boat, kayak, or canoe, choose your own boating adventure in Timucuan Preserve.

title: Hike the Mission Point Trail
accessibility: This is a relatively flat dirt trail. Pine needles or leaves may be on the ground, but otherwise is clear.
short_description: A half-mile loop trail along a relatively flat bluff takes you through standing pine forests to the edge of Lake Roosevelt. From there you can see the site of Kettle Falls, a place used for millennia by the local tribes for salmon fishing.

title: Hike the Rift Zone Trail to the Vedanta Society Retreat Access Road
accessibility: The northern 0.3 miles (0.5 kilometers) of the Rift Zone Trail from the Bear Valley Trailhead is fairly flat, but narrow, only a couple feet across. The trail surface is packed dirt. As the trail progresses, it becomes narrower and rutted in places, and frequently muddy. Short sections of moderate to steep grade exist.
short_description: Explore a section of the floor of a valley that follows the San Andreas Fault, passing through meadows and woods. This trail begins at the Bear Valley Trailhead, at the south end of the Bear Valley Parking Lot.

title: Picnic at the Lehman Caves Picnic Area
accessibility: This area has wheelchair accessible areas with pavement and low grades.
short_description: Picnic Area at Lehman Caves

title: Stones River NB Junior Ranger Program
topics: African American Heritage;National Cemetery;Battlefields;US Army;Civil War
accessibility: An accessible version of our Junior Ranger book is available at Stones River Junior Ranger Activity Book (nps.gov) .
short_description: Become a Stones River National Battlefield Junior Ranger!

title: View Exhibits at the Minidoka Visitor Center
accessibility: The Minidoka Visitor Center has features for visitors with mobility disabilities. The main route from the parking area to the visitor center entrance is wheelchair-friendly, and the main doors feature a push-button opener. The interior of the visitor center is on a single floor level, with no stairs or ramps, and there is ample room to move around museum displays. Most exhibits do not include audio components. No audio description of the exhibit displays are available at this time.
short_description: Much of the Minidoka Visitor Center, located within a historic warehouse, is dedicated to museum exhibits. Displays and historic objects help to tell the story of the Japanese Americans incarcerated here during WWII.

title: Take a Self-Guided Walking Tour of Minidoka
topics: Asian American Heritage;Incarceration;Japanese-American Internment;Civil Rights;World War II
accessibility: Trails at the site are wide but paved with gravel. Gravel is loose in some areas and may be difficult for some visitors to travel on. Most trails are flat, with the exception of a moderate slope when approaching Block 22.
short_description: Minidoka National Historic Site offers 1.6 miles (2.5 km) of gravel walking trails. Visitors may explore the site and the exteriors of historic structures at their own pace. Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information.

title: Take a Short Hike Near the Visitor Center
accessibility: Peabody Creek Trail: This trail is not considered ADA accessible. Visitors should be aware that this trail involves sometimes-steep inclines and declines, steps, and wooden bridge crossings. There are some natural obstacles along the trail route, including tree roots. Living Forest Trail: This trail is considered accessible with assistance. The trail does not meet ADA standards, but may be accessible by visitors with sufficient upper body strength and balance, or a friend to help. Living Forest Trail has an elevation change of 82 feet.
short_description: Near the Olympic National Park Visitor Center, two short loop hikes take visitors through peaceful, green lowland forests.

title: Horse Riding in Point Reyes National Seashore
accessibility: Visitors with their own horses should evaluate accessibility needs prior to arrival in Point Reyes. A mounting block is available at the Bear Valley trailhead. Stop by a visitor center or call 415-464-5100 to speak with a ranger about site-specific accessibility questions. For information about accessibility accomodations on guided trail rides, please call Five Brooks Ranch directly at 415-663-1570 or visit their website.
short_description: Where to go and what to know before exploring Point Reyes from the saddle!

title: Stargazing in Big Cypress
accessibility: All boardwalks, sidewalks, and parking areas are ADA accessible. Areas away from developed viewing places are likely not ADA accesible.
short_description: Dark skies are essential natural, scientific, cultural, and economic resources. National Park sites, including Big Cypress National Preserve, are home to some of the last remaining dark skies in the country and are committed to protecting the night sky resource.

title: Paddling The Riverway
topics: Natural Sounds;Night Sky;River and Riparian;Rock Landscapes and Features;Scenic Views;Water Trails;Watersheds;Wetlands
accessibility: The rivers of the Namekagon and St. Croix consist of rocky and sandy bottoms and large boulders and snags within. River depth varies from ankle deep to 20 to 30 feet deep. The river generally runs as a Class I with a speed of two to three miles an hour. During spring runoff or heavy rain events, the rivers can be Class II or III. Service animals are allowed.
short_description: Paddling the rivers of the St. Croix National Scenic Riverway.

title: Fort Clatsop Audio Tour
topics: Explorers and Expeditions;Forts;Native American Heritage;Westward Expansion
fee_description: One $10 entrance fee is valid for one adult up to seven days at Lewis and Clark National Historical Park. All children ages 15 and under are always admitted free of charge.
accessibility: The trails to Fort Clatsop and the spring are wide and flat, with a woodchip or dirt surface. The trail to the canoe landing is a bit steeper, and can be slick. Electric wheelchairs are available free of charge at all times at the visitor center. They can be taken to the fort and surrounding area, but should not be taken down to the canoe landing. Service animals are welcome in all areas of the park.
short_description: Embark on a voyage of discovery as you learn about the historical homelands of the Clatsop people, and the winter that Lewis and Clark spent in the area. This self-guided audio tour will take you to the must-see sights around Fort Clatsop, beginning at the visitor center and ending back in the parking lot.

title: Walk the Kule Loklo Trail
accessibility: The first part of the 0.4 mile (650 meter) dirt trail to Kule Loklo is quite steep, but then the trail levels off with relatively minimal cross slope. However, the dirt trail does pass over some exposed tree roots, which may be difficult for some to get over. Many gopher holes fill the grassy field at Kule Loklo, making it challenging for some to navigate between the exhibit's structures in a wheelchair or on crutches. There are no accessible restrooms. Inquire at Bear Valley Visitor Center for more information on accessing Kule Loklo.
short_description: A short path leads up to a replica of a Coast Miwok Indian village. Interpretive signs briefly describe Coast Miwok culture and history and the structures in the village. This trail begins at the north end of the Bear Valley parking lot.

title: Hike Emmons Moraine Trail
fee_description: Park entrance fee required
accessibility: The Glacier Basin trail starts out on a relatively flat, smooth, dirt path that gradually ascends through the forest. The spur trail to the Emmons Moraine is more rocky and narrow, with a bridge over the river and a short switchback climbs up loose dirt.
short_description: Enjoy a short hike from the White River Campground through the forest to a view of the Emmons Glacier and a beautiful turquoise lake colored by glacial silt.

title: See Madison Falls
accessibility: A gravel parking lot is located near the trailhead. An accessible vault toilet is located at the trailhead. The trail distance is 0.1 miles, one way. The trail has a gentle slope. Elevation gain is minimal.
short_description: Madison Falls is a stunning 60-foot waterfall near the Elwha River. It's also one of the most accessible destinations at the park, making it a great stop for families and visitors of all abilities.

title: Hike the McClures Beach Trail
season:
Winter

The heaviest rainfall occurs in the winter months. Come prepared for rain and drizzle to possibly last for several days. In between winter rains, it is often sunny, calm, and cool.

Spring

Most spring days are windy and McClures Beach frequently experiences strong breezes. Expect cool temperatures in March. By late May and early June, temperatures can be quite pleasant, even warm.

Summer

Although there is very little rain during summer months, there is often dense fog throughout the day in July, August and September with temperatures often 20 degrees cooler than at Bear Valley.

Fall

The coastal areas of Point Reyes experience some of the clearest days in late September, October and early November. The occasional storm will start rolling through in late October, bringing clouds, wind, and rain. The strongest winds occur in November and December during occasional southerly gales.
accessibility: A moderately steep, narrow dirt trail leads downhill from the paved parking lot at the McClures Beach Trailhead . The lowest section of the trail immediately above the beach may have a steep drop-off or be washed out due to high tides undercutting the trail.
short_description: A rugged trail descends moderately steeply down a ravine to the ocean. McClures Beach is contained within a beautiful cove backed by rocky cliffs, but watch out for tidal fluctuations and dangerous surf. Allow 35 minutes driving time from Bear Valley to the McClures Beach Trailhead, located at the end of the Pierce Point Road, below Pierce Point Ranch to the west.

title: Hike the Emigrant Trail
fee_description: There are no fees charged to enter Hagerman Fossil Beds National Monument.
accessibility: Trail Length: 3.25 mi (5.25 km) one way Cumulative Elevation Change: 560 ft (171 m) Elevation Gain: 600 ft (183 m) Elevation Loss: 40 ft (12 m) Typical Grade: 4.2% Maximum Grade: 21% Typical Cross Slope: 4.6% Typical Tread Width: 4 ft (1.2 m) Obstructions: loose rocks, anthills, animal burrows, vegetation Trail Surface: Packed soil, hard-packed gravel Conditions may have changed since trails were assessed.
short_description: The Emigrant Trail roughly parallels visible remnants of the Oregon Trail, capturing some of the experience of mid-1800s emigrants moving West.

title: Become a Junior Ranger at Reconstruction Era National Historical Park
accessibility: The Junior Ranger booklet is a 9-page book recommended for 7 and up. If you are not able to pick up the book in person, we can mail a booklet to you. If you were not able to finish the book while at the park you can mail it to us, and we will send you a badge.
short_description: Learn how you can earn your Junior Ranger badge at Reconstruction Era National Historical Park.

title: Hike the Gates of Lodore Trail

fee_description: Visitors must pay the park entrance fee or show a valid pass at the Entrance Station or Quarry Visitor Center. There is no separate or additional fee for this activity.
accessibility: The trail is primarily a narrow footpath approximately 2 feet (0.6 m) wide. The surface is a mixture of dirt and rock. The trail does climb several rock stairs. While the trail is rugged and may be difficult to traverse for some individuals with mobility disabilities, the terrain would not preclude those who are willing to take on the challenge. The trail is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: 1 mile (1.6 km) round trip, out and back trail. Easy. The Gates of Lodore Trail is a short but scenic walk to a view of the Green River as it enters the Canyon of Lodore. A trail booklet is available at the Visitor Centers. No pets allowed.

fee_description: Visitors must pay the park entrance fee or show a valid pass at the Entrance Station or Quarry Visitor Center. There is no separate or additional fee for this activity.
accessibility: The trail is primarily a narrow footpath approximately 2 feet (0.6 meters) wide. The surface is a mixture of dirt and rock. There are some steep grades. While the trail is rugged and may be difficult to traverse for some individuals with mobility disabilities, the terrain would not preclude those who are willing to take on the challenge. The trail is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: 2 miles (3.2 km) round trip, out and back trail. Moderate difficulty. The Harpers Corner Trail runs along a narrow ridge to a spectacular viewpoint with views of the rivers far below. Along the way, hikers can gaze across the remote canyon country. A pamphlet for this trail is available at the Visitor Centers. The trail is typically inaccessible in winter. No pets allowed.

title: Hike the Ruple Point Trail

fee_description: Visitors must pay the park entrance fee or show a valid pass at the Entrance Station or Quarry Visitor Center. There is no separate or additional fee for this activity.
accessibility: The trail is primarily a narrow footpath approximately 2 feet (0.6 meters) wide. The surface is a rugged mixture of dirt and rock. Getting to the viewpoint at the end of the trail requires walking up and down over uneven rock surfaces. This trail is not wheelchair accessible.
short_description: 9.2 miles (14.8 km) round trip, out and back trail. Moderate to difficult. For most of its length, Ruple Point Trail crosses a rolling terrain filled with sagebrush and juniper. Near the end, a short descent rewards hikers with a breathtaking views of Split Mountain Canyon and the Green River below. No pets allowed.

title: Hike the Plug Hat Trail

fee_description: Visitors must pay the park entrance fee or show a valid pass at the Entrance Station or Quarry Visitor Center. There is no separate or additional fee for this activity.
accessibility: This trail is paved and accessible to wheelchairs, although some assistance may be required. The paved path is about 3 feet (1 m) wide. There are some gentle bumps and cracks in the pavement. The trail is relatively flat the entire way. Benches are located at scenic viewpoints.
short_description: 0.25 miles (0.4 km) round trip loop trail. Easy. The Plug Hat Trail offers scenic views of Dinosaur's rugged landscape from atop a sandstone butte. This trail is paved and wheelchair accessible. Leashed pets are allowed.

title: Hike the Box Canyon Trail
